reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Symptoms depend on which bowel layer is infiltrated: mucosal disease causes abdominal pain, diarrhoea, vomiting and malabsorption; muscular disease causes obstructive symptoms; and serosal disease produces eosinophilic ascites
Peripheral blood eosinophilia is common but not universal, so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis
Many patients have a personal or family history of atopy, asthma, eczema or food allergy
Diagnosis rests on demonstrating dense eosinophilic infiltration on biopsy after excluding secondary causes such as parasitic infection, drug reaction and connective-tissue disease
Endoscopic appearances range from normal mucosa to erythema, nodularity or ulceration, so multiple biopsies from several sites are needed even when the mucosa looks normal
Serosal disease characteristically presents with eosinophil-rich ascites that improves rapidly with corticosteroids
Management centres on dietary elimination and corticosteroids for eosinophilic gastroenteritis, with corticosteroid-sparing agents reserved for relapsing disease
reference.pathophysiology: Eosinophilic gastroenteritis is characterised by abnormal eosinophil accumulation within the wall of the stomach and small bowel in the absence of an identifiable secondary cause such as parasitic infection or drug reaction. Allergen exposure and a T-helper-2 driven immune response promote release of cytokines such as interleukin-5 and eotaxin, which recruit and activate eosinophils; their degranulation releases toxic granule proteins that damage tissue and cause dysmotility, oedema and increased permeability. The clinical picture is determined by the depth of infiltration, with mucosal, muscular and serosal patterns producing distinct presentations.
additionalDifferentials: Parasitic infection (e.g. strongyloidiasis, anisakiasis) causing tissue eosinophilia
Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive enteropathies
Systemic vasculitis such as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film to detect and quantify peripheral eosinophilia
Upper and lower endoscopy with multiple biopsies from grossly normal and abnormal mucosa
Stool microscopy and serology to exclude parasitic infection
Coeliac serology and total IgE with allergy assessment
Cross-sectional imaging to assess bowel-wall thickening and ascites
Diagnostic paracentesis of ascitic fluid for eosinophil count in suspected serosal disease
redFlags: Features of bowel obstruction suggesting transmural muscular disease
Weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding or a mass raising concern for malignancy
Very high peripheral eosinophil counts suggesting hypereosinophilic syndrome with end-organ damage
reference.prognosis: The condition typically follows a relapsing-remitting course; most patients respond well to dietary and corticosteroid therapy, though some require long-term maintenance treatment, and serosal disease usually responds most briskly.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because peripheral eosinophilia is absent
Taking too few biopsies or sampling only visibly abnormal mucosa and missing patchy infiltration
Attributing tissue eosinophilia to eosinophilic gastroenteritis without excluding parasites, drugs and vasculitis
Overlooking muscular disease as a cause of unexplained obstruction
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
